worked_examples.problem: In-Text Question & Exercise (Section 7.4 & p. 15): (a) What are the functions of the placenta during human gestation? (b) List three different methods of contraception and explain their working mechanisms.
worked_examples.given: Maternal-fetal uterine physiology; Reproductive health and family planning.
worked_examples.formula: Placenta villi countercurrent exchange; Barrier, chemical, and surgical contraceptive mechanisms.
worked_examples.substitution: Nutrient/gas exchange across maternal blood spaces.
worked_examples.calculation:
(a) Functions of Placenta: A specialized disc-shaped vascular organ embedded in the uterine wall. Chorionic villi on the fetal side provide huge surface area in maternal blood pools. Functions: 1. Delivers glucose, amino acids, and oxygen from mother to embryo. 2. Transports metabolic wastes (urea, uric acid, CO2) from embryo to maternal blood for excretion. 3. Endocrine gland secreting progesterone and human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) to maintain pregnancy.
(b) Contraceptive Methods:
1. Barrier Methods (Condoms, diaphragms): Physically prevent sperm from entering the female cervix/uterus, while shielding against Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs).
2. Hormonal / Chemical Methods (Oral contraceptive pills): Ingested hormones alter estrogen-progesterone balance, preventing ovulation from ovaries.
3. Surgical Methods (Vasectomy in males, Tubectomy in females): Tying and cutting the vas deferens or fallopian tubes permanently blocks gamete transit.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Placenta delivers nutrients/oxygen to embryo, removes metabolic wastes, and secretes hormones; (b) Barrier blocks sperm transit, hormonal stops ovulation, surgical cuts/ties gamete conduits.

worked_examples.problem: In-Text Question & Exercise (Section 8.1, 8.2 & p. 6): (a) A Mendelian cross between tall pea plants (TT) and short pea plants (tt) produced all tall plants in the F1 generation. When F1 plants were self-pollinated, what was the ratio of tall to short plants in the F2 generation? (b) How is the sex of a human child determined genetically?
worked_examples.given: Mendelian monohybrid cross; Human chromosomal sex determination.
worked_examples.formula: Monohybrid phenotypic ratio 3 : 1, genotypic ratio 1 : 2 : 1. Sex determination: Female XX, Male XY. Probability of male vs female = 50% each.
worked_examples.substitution: Punnett square analysis: F1 (Tt) x F1 (Tt) -> TT, Tt, Tt, tt.
worked_examples.calculation:
(a) Mendelian Monohybrid Cross:
1. Parents: TT (pure tall) x tt (pure dwarf).
2. Gametes: T and t -> F1 Generation: All Tt (heterozygous tall; 'T' is dominant over recessive 't').
3. Selfing F1 (Tt x Tt):
   Gametes: T, t from both parents.
   F2 Genotypes: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt (Genotypic ratio 1 : 2 : 1).
   F2 Phenotypes: 3 Tall : 1 Short (Phenotypic ratio 3 : 1, i.e. 75% tall, 25% dwarf).
(b) Sex Determination in Humans:
Human females have two homologous X chromosomes (XX), producing only one type of ovum carrying an X chromosome. Human males have heteromorphic sex chromosomes (XY), producing two types of sperm: 50% carry an X chromosome, and 50% carry a Y chromosome.
- If an X-sperm fertilises the ovum: Zygote is XX -> Female child.
- If a Y-sperm fertilises the ovum: Zygote is XY -> Male child.
Since fertilization by X or Y sperm is an equal random probability (50%), the child's genetic sex is determined strictly by the father's fertilising sperm.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) F2 phenotypic ratio is 3 Tall : 1 Short (75% tall, 25% short); (b) Sex is determined by the sperm: X-sperm produces a girl (XX), Y-sperm produces a boy (XY) with 50% probability.

title: Reflection of Light and Plane Mirrors
description: Master the foundational laws of reflection, characteristics of plane mirrors, and curved reflecting surfaces.
ai_system_prompt_context:
CBSE Class 10 Science Module 1: Reflection of Light and Plane Mirrors. Mid-Term Examination Syllabus. Emphasize normal drawing in reflection. Practice angle calculations where angle with the mirror surface is given.
TEXTBOOK GROUNDING & MANDATORY TEACHING DIRECTIVES (PHASE 5 20-MINUTE MASTER CLASS):
- Capsule Duration: 20 Minutes (Full comprehensive lesson covering all textbook nuances)
- Capsule Overview Diagram: Plane mirror surface, normal line perpendicular, incident ray with arrow, reflected ray with arrow, angle i and angle r labeled.
- Diagram Type: vector_svg_diagram
- Chapter Multi-Level Flowchart: Light Propagation -> Rectilinear Path -> Reflection -> Laws of Reflection (i = r, Coplanar) -> Plane vs Curved Surfaces
- FLOWCHART DIRECTIVE: Call write_chalkboard(action="draw_flowchart", content="Light Propagation -> Rectilinear Path -> Reflection -> Laws of Reflection (i = r, Coplanar) -> Plane vs Curved Surfaces") to visually organize the concepts on the board!

- Verbatim Textbook Definitions:
- Laws of Reflection: "The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, normal, and reflected ray lie in the same plane." [SI Unit: Degrees (°)]

- Textbook Concrete Examples:
- Activity 9.1 (Shining Spoon): Viewing your face in the curved inward and outward surfaces of a large shining spoon.


- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:
  * Concept #1 "Law of Reflection 1: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection (i = r).":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of 30° with the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: 60°
      -> Socratic Hint: Remember that the angle of incidence is measured with respect to the normal (perpendicular to the surface), not the mirror surface itself!
    * [Q2] (2-mark Definition): State the two laws of reflection of light.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: (1) The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. (2) The incident ray, normal to the mirror at the point of incidence, and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.
      -> Socratic Hint: Recite both the angular equality and the coplanar requirement.
  * Concept #2 "Plane Mirror Image Properties":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): If an object is placed 10 cm in front of a plane mirror, what is the distance between the object and its image?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: 20 cm
      -> Socratic Hint: The image is formed as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Calculate total distance object-to-image.
    * [Q2] (PYQ): Why is the image formed by a plane mirror called a virtual image?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Because the light rays do not actually intersect at the image position; they only appear to diverge from it, and it cannot be caught on a screen.
      -> Socratic Hint: Think about whether light rays physically pass through the image location behind the mirror.

- CONCEPT-BY-CONCEPT VISUAL PLAYBOOK (MANDATORY UNIQUE DRAWINGS):
  * Concept #1 "Law of Reflection 1: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection (i = r).":
    - Visual Title: "Laws of Reflection Geometry" (vector_svg_diagram)
    - Why Needed: Visualizes angle measurement relative to the normal.
    - What to Explain: Show students that i and r are always measured from the dashed normal line.
    - Timing & Directive: Present at start of class when discussing reflection laws.
    - Interactive Math Formula: i = r

- MANDATORY WHITEBOARD INSTRUCTION: Each concept in this capsule has a DISTINCT, dedicated visual. You MUST call render_svg_diagram or draw_graph with that concept's UNIQUE diagram when teaching it! NEVER duplicate or reuse the same diagram across different concepts!
- STRICT SOCRATIC PROGRESSION GATING: After teaching each concept in small bites of 2-3 sentences, you MUST pose at least one of the prepared 4-6 exam questions above to the student. You MUST strictly wait for the student to answer or explicitly ask for the answer before advancing to the next concept! Never lecture continuously without student response.
- EXPLANATION MANDATE: When explaining definitions, formulas, and algebraic transitions, unpack the physical meaning and the "why" behind each line out loud. Never merely recite the text!
key_concepts: Law of Reflection 1: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection (i = r).
Law of Reflection 2: Incident ray, normal, and reflected ray lie in the same plane.
Plane Mirror Image Properties: Virtual, erect, laterally inverted, same size, and at equal distance behind the mirror.
success_criteria: Calculate angles of incidence/reflection and explain lateral inversion in plane mirrors.
subtopics: Nature of light and straight-line propagation
Characteristics of images formed by plane mirrors
chapter_notes: Light is an electromagnetic radiation that enables us to see. By observing common optical phenomena, we conclude that light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation), indicated as a ray of light. When light falls on a polished surface like a mirror, reflection occurs obeying the laws of reflection: (i) Angle i = Angle r, and (ii) Incident ray, normal, and reflected ray are coplanar. Plane mirrors produce virtual, erect, laterally inverted images of the same size placed at an equal distance behind the mirror. Curved surfaces (like a shining spoon in Activity 9.1) distort or scale images differently, paving the way for spherical mirrors.

worked_examples.given: Angle with surface = 40°
worked_examples.formula: Angle of incidence i = 90° - (Angle with surface); i = r
worked_examples.problem: A light ray makes an angle of 40° with a plane reflecting surface. Find the angle of reflection.
worked_examples.calculation: Since angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, r = 50°.

common_misconceptions: Confusing angle of incidence with the angle made with the mirror surface.
Believing plane mirror images are real because we see them.

questions.question: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of 30° with the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.socratic_hint: Remember that the angle of incidence is measured with respect to the normal (perpendicular to the surface), not the mirror surface itself!

questions.question: State the two laws of reflection of light.
questions.ideal_answer: (1) The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. (2) The incident ray, normal to the mirror at the point of incidence, and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.
questions.socratic_hint: Recite both the angular equality and the coplanar requirement.

concept_questions.concept_title: Law of Reflection 1: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection (i = r).

questions.question: If an object is placed 10 cm in front of a plane mirror, what is the distance between the object and its image?
questions.ideal_answer: 20 cm
questions.socratic_hint: The image is formed as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Calculate total distance object-to-image.

questions.question: Why is the image formed by a plane mirror called a virtual image?
questions.ideal_answer: Because the light rays do not actually intersect at the image position; they only appear to diverge from it, and it cannot be caught on a screen.
questions.socratic_hint: Think about whether light rays physically pass through the image location behind the mirror.

title: Spherical Mirrors: Terminology and Focus
description: Understand concave and convex mirrors, poles, centres of curvature, principal axes, and principal foci.
ai_system_prompt_context:
CBSE Class 10 Science Module 2: Spherical Mirrors: Terminology and Focus. Mid-Term Examination Syllabus. Clearly distinguish between real focus of concave mirrors and virtual focus of convex mirrors using diagrams.
TEXTBOOK GROUNDING & MANDATORY TEACHING DIRECTIVES (PHASE 5 20-MINUTE MASTER CLASS):
- Capsule Duration: 20 Minutes (Full comprehensive lesson covering all textbook nuances)
- Capsule Overview Diagram: Concave mirror with parallel rays converging at F; Convex mirror with parallel rays diverging from F behind the mirror.
- Diagram Type: ray_optics
- Chapter Multi-Level Flowchart: Spherical Mirror -> Concave (Inward) | Convex (Outward) -> Terms: P, C, R, F, f -> Relation: R = 2f
- FLOWCHART DIRECTIVE: Call write_chalkboard(action="draw_flowchart", content="Spherical Mirror -> Concave (Inward) | Convex (Outward) -> Terms: P, C, R, F, f -> Relation: R = 2f") to visually organize the concepts on the board!

- Verbatim Textbook Definitions:
- Principal Focus (Concave): "The point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the principal axis actually meet after reflection." [SI Unit: Metres (m) or Centimetres (cm)]

- Textbook Concrete Examples:
- Activity 9.2: Focusing sunlight using a concave mirror to burn a paper and find approximate focal length.

- AUTHENTIC TEXTBOOK EXERCISES & QUESTIONS:
  - In-text Q (Page 142):
    * [Q1] (conceptual): Define the principal focus of a concave mirror.
      Method: State that parallel rays converge at a specific point on the principal axis.
    * [Q2] (numerical): The radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is 20 cm. What is its focal length?
      Method: Use f = R/2 -> 20/2 = 10 cm.

- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:
  * Concept #1 "Concave Mirror":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): Which of the following mirrors is a converging mirror?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Concave mirror
      -> Socratic Hint: Think about how parallel rays behave when striking a concave mirror versus a convex mirror.
    * [Q2] (2-mark Definition): Define the pole of a spherical mirror.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: The centre of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror is a point called the pole (P). It lies on the surface of the mirror.
      -> Socratic Hint: Where is the geometric center of the mirror's reflecting face?
  * Concept #2 "Radius and Focal Length Relation: R = 2f for mirrors of small aperture.":
    * [Q1] (5-mark Numerical): The radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is 20 cm. What is its focal length?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: f = R / 2 = 20 cm / 2 = 10 cm.
      -> Socratic Hint: Use the formula connecting focal length f and radius of curvature R.

- CONCEPT-BY-CONCEPT VISUAL PLAYBOOK (MANDATORY UNIQUE DRAWINGS):
  * Concept #1 "Concave Mirror":
    - Visual Title: "Concave Mirror Principal Focus" (ray_optics)
    - Why Needed: Demonstrates converging nature of concave mirrors.
    - What to Explain: Parallel rays converge at F in front of the mirror.
    - Timing & Directive: Show when discussing focal length and focus definition.
    - Interactive Math Formula: f = R/2

- MANDATORY WHITEBOARD INSTRUCTION: Each concept in this capsule has a DISTINCT, dedicated visual. You MUST call render_svg_diagram or draw_graph with that concept's UNIQUE diagram when teaching it! NEVER duplicate or reuse the same diagram across different concepts!
- STRICT SOCRATIC PROGRESSION GATING: After teaching each concept in small bites of 2-3 sentences, you MUST pose at least one of the prepared 4-6 exam questions above to the student. You MUST strictly wait for the student to answer or explicitly ask for the answer before advancing to the next concept! Never lecture continuously without student response.
- EXPLANATION MANDATE: When explaining definitions, formulas, and algebraic transitions, unpack the physical meaning and the "why" behind each line out loud. Never merely recite the text!
key_concepts: Concave Mirror: Spherical mirror with reflecting surface curved inwards.
Convex Mirror: Spherical mirror with reflecting surface curved outwards.
Radius and Focal Length Relation: R = 2f for mirrors of small aperture.
success_criteria: Relate focal length and radius of curvature using R = 2f.
subtopics: Definition of concave and convex mirrors
Key terms: Pole (P), Centre of Curvature (C), Radius of Curvature (R)
chapter_notes: Spherical mirrors have reflecting surfaces that form part of a sphere. A concave mirror curves inwards towards the sphere's centre, while a convex mirror curves outwards. Key terminology includes: Pole (P, centre of reflecting surface), Centre of Curvature (C, centre of the hollow sphere), Radius of Curvature (R, radius of the sphere), Principal Axis (straight line passing through P and C), Principal Focus (F, point where parallel rays converge or appear to diverge), and Focal Length (f, distance between P and F). For small apertures, R = 2f.

worked_examples.given: R = +32 cm (convex mirror)
worked_examples.formula: f = R / 2
worked_examples.problem: Find the focal length of a convex mirror whose radius of curvature is 32 cm.
worked_examples.calculation: f = 16 cm
worked_examples.finalAnswer: +16 cm

common_misconceptions: Confusing focus position for convex mirrors (virtual focus behind mirror) with concave mirrors (real focus in front).
Forgetting sign conventions when applying R = 2f.

title: Image Formation by Spherical Mirrors and Mirror Formula
description: Master ray diagram rules, image characteristics tables, sign conventions, mirror formula, and magnification.
ai_system_prompt_context:
CBSE Class 10 Science Module 3: Image Formation by Spherical Mirrors and Mirror Formula. Mid-Term Examination Syllabus. Strictly enforce the New Cartesian Sign Convention before substituting values into the mirror formula.
TEXTBOOK GROUNDING & MANDATORY TEACHING DIRECTIVES (PHASE 5 20-MINUTE MASTER CLASS):
- Capsule Duration: 20 Minutes (Full comprehensive lesson covering all textbook nuances)
- Capsule Overview Diagram: Cartesian coordinate system centered at pole P, showing positive x, negative x, positive y, negative y quadrants for reflection.
- Diagram Type: vector_svg_diagram
- Chapter Multi-Level Flowchart: Spherical Mirrors -> Ray Rules (1, 2, 3, 4) -> Sign Convention (Cartesian) -> Mirror Formula (1/v + 1/u = 1/f) -> Magnification (m = -v/u)
- FLOWCHART DIRECTIVE: Call write_chalkboard(action="draw_flowchart", content="Spherical Mirrors -> Ray Rules (1, 2, 3, 4) -> Sign Convention (Cartesian) -> Mirror Formula (1/v + 1/u = 1/f) -> Magnification (m = -v/u)") to visually organize the concepts on the board!

- Verbatim Textbook Definitions:
- Mirror Formula: "1/v + 1/u = 1/f, relating object distance u, image distance v, and focal length f." [SI Unit: Dimensionless relation]

- Textbook Concrete Examples:
- Example 9.1: Convex mirror rear-view calculation with R = 3.00 m and object distance u = -5.00 m.
- Example 9.2: Concave mirror screen placement and image size calculation for object at 25 cm.

- AUTHENTIC TEXTBOOK EXERCISES & QUESTIONS:
  - End of Chapter Q7:
    * [Q7] (conceptual): We wish to obtain an erect image of an object, using a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. What should be the range of distance of the object from the mirror?
      Method: Between pole P and focus F (0 to 15 cm).

- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:

chapter_notes: Image formation in spherical mirrors uses ray diagrams governed by four key rules: (i) Parallel rays pass through focus F, (ii) Rays through focus emerge parallel, (iii) Rays through centre of curvature C reflect back along the same path, and (iv) Oblique rays at pole P reflect at equal angles. The New Cartesian Sign Convention sets pole P as origin, object on the left, distances measured right as positive, left as negative, heights above principal axis positive, and below negative. The mirror formula is 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = h'/h = -v/u.

ai_system_prompt_context:

- Snell's Law: "sin i / sin r = constant (refractive index of second medium with respect to first)." [SI Unit: Dimensionless]

- Textbook Concrete Examples:

- AUTHENTIC TEXTBOOK EXERCISES & QUESTIONS:

    * [Q2] (numerical): Light enters from air to glass having refractive index 1.50. What is the speed of light in the glass?

- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:

      -> Ideal Model Answer: The ratio of the sine of angle of incidence to the sine of angle of refraction is a constant for a given pair of media and given color of light (sin i / sin r = constant).
      -> Socratic Hint: Mention sines of angles i and r and the constant term.
  * Concept #2 "Absolute Refractive Index (n): Ratio of speed of light in vacuum/air to speed of light in the medium (n = c / v).":
    * [Q1] (5-mark Numerical): Light enters from air to glass having refractive index 1.50. What is the speed of light in the glass? (Speed of light in vacuum = 3 × 10^8 m/s)
      -> Ideal Model Answer: 2 × 10^8 m/s
      -> Socratic Hint: Use n = c / v rearranged as v = c / n.

key_concepts: Snell's Law of Refraction: The ratio of the sine of angle of incidence to the sine of angle of refraction is a constant (sin i / sin r = n21).
Absolute Refractive Index (n): Ratio of speed of light in vacuum/air to speed of light in the medium (n = c / v).
Bending Rule: Rarer to denser bends towards normal; denser to rarer bends away from normal.

chapter_notes: Refraction is the change in direction of light when it travels obliquely from one transparent medium to another, caused by a change in the speed of light. Laws of refraction: (i) Incident ray, refracted ray, and normal are coplanar, and (ii) Snell's law: sin i / sin r = constant (n21). Absolute refractive index nm = c / v. Optically denser medium has a higher refractive index where light slows down and bends towards the normal. Kerosene has higher optical density than water despite lower mass density.

key_concepts: Convex Lens: Thicker at the middle, converges light rays (converging lens).
Concave Lens: Thicker at the edges, diverges light rays (diverging lens).

chapter_notes: Spherical lenses are transparent materials bound by two surfaces, at least one of which is spherical. Convex lenses converge parallel rays to focus F2 and are thicker in the middle. Concave lenses diverge parallel rays appearing from F1 and are thicker at the edges. Optical centre O is the central point where rays pass undeviated. Lenses have two principal foci (F1 and F2). Ray rules for lenses: (i) Parallel rays pass through F2 (or diverge from F1), (ii) Rays through focus emerge parallel, and (iii) Rays through optical centre O pass straight without deviation.

chapter_notes: The lens formula is 1/v - 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = h'/h = v/u. Power of a lens P is the reciprocal of focal length in metres: P = 1 / f. The SI unit of power is dioptre (D), where 1 D = 1 m^-1. Convex lenses have positive power, and concave lenses have negative power. When lenses are placed in contact, net power is the algebraic sum of individual powers: P = P1 + P2 + P3 + ...

worked_examples.problem: In-Text Question (Section 9.2, p. 12): A concave mirror produces three times magnified real image of an object placed at 10 cm in front of it. Where is the image located? What is the focal length of the mirror?
worked_examples.given: Object distance u = -10 cm (sign convention); Magnification m = -3 (real, inverted image).
worked_examples.formula: Magnification $m = -\frac{v}{u}$; Mirror Formula: $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u}$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Image distance: $v = -30\text{ cm}$ (located 30 cm in front of the concave mirror on the same side as object).
2. Focal length:
   $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{-30} + \frac{1}{-10} = \frac{-1 - 3}{30} = \frac{-4}{30} = -\frac{2}{15}$.
   $f = -\frac{15}{2} = -7.5\text{ cm}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Image is located at 30 cm in front of the mirror (v = -30 cm); Focal length of the mirror is -7.5 cm.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Concave mirror real magnified image ray diagram
worked_examples.image_search_query: concave mirror real magnified image ray diagram optics

worked_examples.problem: In-Text Question (Section 9.3, p. 17): Light enters from air to glass having refractive index 1.50. What is the speed of light in glass? (Speed of light in vacuum c = 3 * 10^8 m s^-1).
worked_examples.given: Refractive index of glass n = 1.50; Speed of light in vacuum $c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
worked_examples.formula: Absolute Refractive Index $n = \frac{c}{v} \implies v = \frac{c}{n}$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The speed of light in glass is 2.0 * 10^8 m s^-1.
worked_examples.image_search_query: refraction of light speed in medium snell law calculation

worked_examples.problem: End-of-Chapter Exercise Q10 (p. 26): An object 5 cm in length is held 25 cm away from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Draw the ray diagram and find the position, size, and the nature of the image formed.
worked_examples.given: Object height $h_1 = +5\text{ cm}$; Object distance $u = -25\text{ cm}$; Focal length of convex lens $f = +10\text{ cm}$.
worked_examples.formula: Lens Formula: $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} \implies \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f} + \frac{1}{u}$; Magnification $m = \frac{v}{u} = \frac{h_2}{h_1}$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Image distance: $v = +\frac{50}{3} \approx +16.67\text{ cm}$ (formed on opposite side of lens, real).
2. Image height: $h_2 = h_1 \times \frac{v}{u} = 5 \times \frac{50/3}{-25} = 5 \times \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) = -\frac{10}{3} \approx -3.33\text{ cm}$.
3. Nature: Real, inverted, and diminished (height 3.33 cm).
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Image is real, inverted, located at +16.67 cm behind the lens with height -3.33 cm.

questions.question: A concave lens has focal length of 15 cm. At what distance should the object from the lens be placed so that it forms an image at 10 cm from the lens?
questions.ideal_answer: u = -30 cm
questions.socratic_hint: Use the lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with v = -10 cm and f = -15 cm.

concept_questions.concept_title: Lens Formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f connecting object distance u, image distance v, and focal length f for lenses.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of power of a lens?
questions.ideal_answer: Dioptre (D)
questions.socratic_hint: Recall the unit defined for 1 / f where f is in meters.

questions.question: Find the focal length of a lens of power -2.0 D. What type of lens is this?
questions.ideal_answer: f = -0.50 m (-50 cm); Concave lens.
questions.socratic_hint: Use f = 1 / P. Negative power implies a concave lens.
